Reviewer #1:

The authors have used iTRAQ MS, far Western blotting with purified SH2 domains, and single molecule imaging of SH2 domain-tdEOS fusion protein recruitment to the membrane, to monitor the kinetics of tyrosine phosphorylation events in A431 cells following EGF treatment. Each approach gives complementary results, with surprisingly different response kinetics. The authors discuss the limitations of each method and how together they help build a picture of the cellular response. The new findings include a transient dip in most MS detected sites 2-10 min after EGF. This may be due to recruitment of SH2-containing phosphatases. They also found discrepancies between the phosphorylation of individual sites detected by MS versus phospho antibodies. Perhaps most notably, SH2 binding sites, detected by Far Western, are apparently created more rapidly than SH2-tdEos fusions are recruited to the membrane. The latter may be limited by the time taken to form receptor clusters in the membrane.

The results are interesting in light of the many previous studies of EGF-stimulated tyrosine phosphorylation events. The paper may be a valuable resource for other investigators using this system. However, there are some major issues that weaken the results and lower the significance.

1) The authors used A431 cells, which have a hyper-abundance of EGFRs and are growth inhibited (not stimulated) at the EGF concentration used. This allowed them to follow more phosphorylation events but is of doubtful significance for cells that respond positively to EGF.

2) The responses detected by Far Western blotting were more rapid and had higher dynamic range than those detected by MS, and are faster than SH2-tdEos recruitment in vivo. This may in part be due to the use of clustered SH2 domains to probe the blots (GST-SH2, anti-GST-HRP and GSH-HRP), which will increase avidity and likely cause marked non-linearity in binding, amplifying the signal. Controls with monovalent SH2 domains should be done. The phosphoprotein targets are of course also denatured. It might be more informative to follow association of the endogenous full length proteins by conventional co-IP.

3) The membrane recruitment of fluorescent SH2 domains in vivo was analyzed both by conventional TIRF, providing on- and off-kinetics for net membrane association, and by single molecule PALM, allowing measurement of the number of molecules binding and releasing per unit time, cluster size and diffusion in the plane of the membrane (related to clustering). Based on this they conclude that SH2 domains only bind stably to clustered receptors (due to rebinding and hence low off rate), and that the slow formation of clusters slows down membrane association. This principle was already investigated in the authors' nice PNAS paper (Oh et al. 2012). However, the results don't exclude the possibility that the on-rate to EGFR clusters may also be low. Since EGFR clustering leaves more EGFR-free membrane area, a decrease in on-rate is not unreasonable. It may be possible to measure on-rate to a cluster by photo-converting a cluster and looking at new molecule binding.

Reviewer #2:

This is a very interesting and comprehensive study of the interaction of different phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domains to proteins phosphorylated in response to EGF addition to A431 cells. The paper is technically excellent and is very well written. I had no trouble following the logic of both the experiments and the interpretations. The strengths of the paper include its use of multiple technical approaches to follow both protein phosphorylation and the dynamic interaction of different SH2 domains to their targets, its comprehensive nature and the excellent data sets included with this study (Table 1 makes the entire study worthwhile, in my opinion). The combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches for following binding kinetics is a particular strength.

Where this paper falls short is in placing their results into the context of what is already known and in understanding the consequences of using A431 cells, which have enormous numbers of EGFR.

Their basic conclusion is that clustering of the EGFR affects the ability of SH2-domain proteins to bind and dissociate from the membrane. If the receptors are diffusely distributed, binding is fast. If they are clustered, it is delayed. The reverse rate is also slower if the receptors are clustered. Both of these effects of high receptor density or clustering can be due to diffusion-limited binding, which has been well studied since the seminal work of Berg and Purcell over 35 years ago (Biophy J., 20:193-219, 1977). Although previous studies on the effect of high receptor density and clustering have focused on ligands, binding of SH2-domains should be similar. Indeed, those studies have described the same sort of effects that are described here (e.g., Potanin et al., [1994] Eur Biophys J 23, 197; Lagerholm and Thompson [1998] Biophys J 74, 1215; Gopalakrishnan et al., [2005] Biophys J 89, 3686). For example, although the "apparent binding rates" of SH2-domain proteins to clustered receptors are reduced relative to unclustered receptors, this is because clustered sites compete with each other for binding to diffusing ligands. Dissociation rates look slower because of rebinding effects, and so forth. Diffusion-limited binding of EGF has even been explored in A431 cells because of their extraordinary number of EGFR (see Wiley [1988] J Cell Biol 107, 801). I am not suggesting that these previous studies make the findings presented here superfluous, but they have direct relevance for interpreting their results, especially the effect of clustered density versus total receptor density and the effect of time-dependent receptor occupancy versus time-dependent SH2-domain protein binding. For example, because of diffusion-limited binding of EGF to A431 cells, total receptor occupancy will climb continuously over time rather than rapidly reaching equilibrium (see Figure 2 of Wiley [1988]). This looks very similar to the continuous increase in specific EGFR phosphorylation over time in Figure 3. The "oscillation" they report in the tyrosine phosphorylation levels after stimulation with EGF is thus likely due to a rapid desensitization of the initially activated receptors followed by a slow accumulation of additionally occupied receptors.

Because of diffusion-limited binding, there are three processes they must untangle: 1) the effect of a continuously increasing number of occupied EGFR over time, 2) the time-dependent change in the overall density of activated receptors at the cell surface and its effect on receptor clustering, and 3) the density of receptors in the clusters. All three of these processes will be dependent on the levels of occupied receptors, which unfortunately, were not examined in this paper. Without knowing this information, it is difficult to know whether the types of effects seen here (e.g. Figure 5) are also present in cells lacking EGFR amplification. It’s not necessarily a bad thing if these effects are only seen in EGFR-amplified cells, but this knowledge would certainly help the reader know how widely their results can be extrapolated to other systems. I would suggest that they quantify the time-dependent change in EGFR occupancy in their cells using fluorescently-labeled EGF (available commercially) and show that the range of receptor occupancy they are observing is within the range of other cells. Alternately, they could show that doses of EGF that result in lower levels of net occupancy produce similar results. At the very least, they need to incorporate the previous literature on diffusion-limited binding processes in their Discussion.

Reviewer #3:

Jadwin et al. present a comprehensive analysis of EGF-stimulated phosphorylation and associated SH2/PTB interaction datasets, and was a pleasure to read. The model cell system is the cancer-derived cell line A431, which is known to express high level wild type EGFR (>1-million per cell). The authors are experienced and credible in the field, and in this instance sought to address outstanding questions related to SH2/PTB-mediated signaling downstream of activated EGFR, but generally relevant to tyrosine kinase signaling. Far western analysis showed positively correlated kinetics of binding of a set of domains to proteins known to be tyrosine phosphorylated in response to EGFR activation. These data are complemented by MS-based analysis of individual phospho-peptides, and by measurement of membrane recruitment of ectopically expressed domains. Overall, the authors present interesting data, and Table 1 stands out as an engaging, interactive tool. A main conclusion drawn is that the integration of orthogonal datasets is an effective approach to reveal discrepancies that may relate to technical limitations or possibly biological mechanisms.

In some instances the presentation and discussion of data lack clarity, and there is considerable speculation based on technical phenomenology.

1) The coverage of EGFR phosphorylation sites, central to the study, was not as exhaustive as many published reports, and was not clearly acknowledged/presented or discussed. For example, they describe five different EGFR phosphopeptides, but three are phospho-isomers that contain pY1045. A peptide singularly phosphorylated at the primary GRB2 SH2 site pY1068 was not part of the data, which compromises the interpretation of results and discussions about GRB2.

2) Obviously FW and MS analyses, by technical design, measure different features, but the assumptions associated with these methods should be more thoroughly addressed.

3) Some conclusion statements reiterate consensus views, and hence would be appropriate for the Introduction. Examples include:

"…suggests that the concentration of SH2 domain binding sites can be as important as SH2 domain binding specificity…"

"…suggest that the stoichiometry of SH2 and PTB domain-containing effectors bound to EGFR is temporally regulated by differential phosphorylation/dephosphorylation of their specific binding sites…"

"…these data suggest that EGFR overexpression is associated with a significant expansion of its classical downstream signal transduction pathways"

4) What are the estimated concentrations of ectopic domains versus endogenous? For example, is competition between ectopic GRB2 SH2 with endogenous GRB2, which is reportedly highly expressed (approx. 500K/Hela cell), factored into the calculations and data interpretation?

5) The interpretation that the pervanadate effect is due to a lack of clustering is speculative. What is the (enhanced) stoichiometry/level of phosphorylation in response to pervanadate compared with EGF?

results.result: Far-Western blotting of EGF-stimulated A431 cells identified 27 SH2/PTB probes with dynamic binding patterns. Five major phosphoproteins (EGFR, p130CAS doublet, GAB1, and SHCA) were identified with distinct phosphorylation kinetics following EGF treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 describe the far-Western methodology and identify major phosphoproteins with distinct temporal patterns. The experimental approach is well-documented with appropriate controls (C20), and protein identities were confirmed by immunodepletion (C22). The kinetic patterns are supported by data in Figure 2A and supplements.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering identified six distinct SH2 domain-binding clusters with binding patterns consistent with known interactions. After normalization to pY abundance, most SH2 domains showed higher relative affinity for GAB1 and p130CAS rather than EGFR.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 describe clustering analysis that groups SH2 domains by binding specificity. The results are consistent with literature (C28-C30) and reveal that EGFR dominance in raw data is due to abundance rather than specificity (C32-C33). The normalization approach is methodologically sound.

results.result: Phosphosite-specific Western blotting revealed that different EGFR sites are phosphorylated with different kinetics. EGFR pY992 kinetics correlated with CRKL binding (R²=0.88), pY1068 with GRB2 binding (R²=0.91), and total EGFR pY with SHCA PTB binding (R²=0.89). ERK1/2 activation peaked at ~4 min, later than EGFR phosphorylation at 1.5-2 min.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate site-specific phosphorylation dynamics that correlate with SH2 domain binding patterns. The strong correlations (R²>0.85) between specific phosphosites and cognate SH2 domains validate both the far-Western approach and the biological specificity. The ERK activation timing provides functional context.

results.result: iTRAQ mass spectrometry identified 132 unique pY sites from 93 proteins, with 88 sites (67 proteins) showing EGF-dependent increases. The proportion of EGF-dependent sites (65%) was higher than in previous studies, and 64 sites from 57 proteins were not previously documented as EGF-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 describe comprehensive MS analysis with clear statistical criteria for EGF-dependence (C39). The higher proportion of EGF-dependent sites compared to previous studies (C40) is appropriately attributed to EGFR overexpression in A431 cells. Discovery of 64 novel EGF-dependent sites (C41) represents a significant contribution.

results.result: Gene ontology analysis revealed functional differences between EGF-responsive and non-responsive phosphoproteins. EGF-responsive proteins were enriched for signaling regulation terms, while non-responsive proteins were associated with cell adhesion and locomotion. EGF-nonresponsive sites were enriched for CRK binding motifs (pYXDP/L), while EGF-responsive peptides showed little sequence consensus.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 describe functional annotation of phosphoproteins identified by MS. The GO analysis appropriately distinguishes EGF-responsive from non-responsive proteins (C42-C43), and motif analysis (C44-C45) provides mechanistic insight consistent with the functional associations. The lack of consensus in EGF-responsive peptides suggests diverse signaling mechanisms.

results.result: Comparison of MS phosphopeptide kinetics with far-Western and anti-pY blotting revealed discrepancies for major phosphoproteins. EGFR and SHCA phosphopeptides showed slower kinetics than far-Western, GAB1 peptides did not show rapid dephosphorylation seen in far-Western, and p130CAS peptides did not recapitulate the dephosphorylation/rephosphorylation pattern. Most phosphopeptides showed a transient decrease at 3 min similar to far-Western data.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 document important methodological differences between MS and far-Western approaches. The discrepancies are clearly described and appropriately interpreted as reflecting differences in what each method measures (C92). The observation of a common 3-min dip across methods (C52) validates that both approaches capture real biological dynamics.

results.result: Live cell imaging revealed distinct recruitment patterns for different SH2 domains. GAB1-binding domains showed rapid recruitment and diffusion with diffuse localization, EGFR-binding domains showed slow recruitment and clustering, and p130CAS-binding domains showed slow or minimal recruitment to focal adhesions. Recruitment time constants negatively correlated with diffusion rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 describe in vivo SH2 domain behavior using live cell imaging. The patterns are consistent with binding specificities determined by far-Western (C53-C55). The negative correlation between recruitment kinetics and diffusion (C57) suggests a mechanistic link. EGF binding kinetics matched far-Western data (C56), validating the experimental system.

results.result: In vivo SH2 domain membrane recruitment was significantly slower than binding site creation measured by far-Western. Time constants from live cell imaging were ~6 times greater than from far-Western, indicating that SH2 membrane recruitment is not in rapid equilibrium with tyrosine phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 and C93-C94 describe the central unexpected finding of delayed in vivo recruitment. The quantitative comparison is well-documented (Table 1), and multiple control experiments ruled out technical artifacts (C60-C63). This represents a major discovery about SH2 domain binding dynamics in living cells.

results.result: Multiple control experiments ruled out technical explanations for delayed in vivo recruitment. GRB2 SH2-tdEOS (6.5 μM) and pY-EGFR (1.5 μM) concentrations were sufficient for rapid equilibration. Apical and basal membrane phosphorylation kinetics were similar. Far-Western signals were not saturated. At lower EGF concentration (1 ng/ml, mitogenic), the delay was reduced but still present (~2-fold vs ~7.5-fold at 25 ng/ml).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 describe rigorous control experiments addressing potential artifacts. The biochemical measurements (C60-C61), confocal microscopy (C62), serial dilution experiments (C63), and dose-response studies (C64-C66) systematically rule out alternative explanations. The persistence of delay at mitogenic EGF concentrations (C66) suggests biological relevance.

results.result: NCK1 SH2 domain showed an initial decrease in membrane binding upon EGF treatment, consistent with far-Western data showing decreased p130CAS phosphorylation. Both NCK1 SH2 and p130CAS localized to focal adhesion-like structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 describe an exception to the general pattern where in vivo binding matched the decrease seen in far-Western. The localization to focal adhesions (C68) is consistent with p130CAS biology and validates the specificity of the NCK1 SH2 domain probe.

results.result: Single-molecule tracking revealed that GRB2 SH2 binding rate increased rapidly (τ=2.08 min), much faster than total binding. Cluster formation reached maximum at 10-15 min, coincident with maximal membrane recruitment. Binding to non-clustered sites was fast (τ=1.08 min), while binding within clusters was slow (τ=4.05 min), suggesting that delayed recruitment results from slow accumulation of clustered binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 provide mechanistic insight into delayed recruitment through spatial analysis. The sptPALM data clearly distinguish clustered from non-clustered binding (C72-C73), and the temporal correlation between clustering and recruitment (C70) supports the mechanistic interpretation (C74). This represents a key advance in understanding the delay.

results.result: Pervanadate treatment, which increases phosphorylation without inducing receptor clustering, resulted in rapid GRB2 SH2 recruitment (τ=0.81 min) comparable to binding site creation kinetics. GRB2 SH2 showed diffuse distribution and high mobility in PV-treated cells, confirming lack of clustering. This demonstrates that delayed recruitment in EGF-treated cells results from binding site clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 describe a critical experiment that directly tests the clustering hypothesis. The PV treatment provides high phosphorylation without clustering (C75-C79), and the resulting rapid recruitment (C80-C81) that matches binding site creation strongly supports the clustering mechanism (C82). This is compelling evidence for the central conclusion.

results.result: Integration of far-Western, MS, and live cell imaging revealed that in vivo SH2 binding is much slower than binding site creation, and delayed recruitment correlates with clustering of binding sites on the membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 summarize the main findings from the multimodal approach. The integration of three complementary methods (C83) revealed the unexpected delay (C84) and its correlation with clustering (C85). This represents the core contribution of the study.

results.result: EGFR overexpression in A431 cells is associated with expansion of downstream signaling pathways. Both SH2 domain specificity and binding site concentration determine signaling output, consistent with the concept that signaling pathways can be 're-wired' by dysregulated RTK activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 provide biological context for the findings. The inference about pathway expansion (C86) is supported by the high proportion of EGF-dependent sites and novel phosphosites. The principle that both specificity and concentration matter (C87) is well-supported by the far-Western data, and the pathway rewiring concept (C88) is appropriately cited.

results.result: For multiply phosphorylated proteins, far-Western provides a more complete picture than phosphosite-specific Western blotting alone. The damped oscillation in phosphorylation after EGF stimulation likely reflects rapid feedback mechanisms. Discrepancies between MS and far-Western arise when detected phosphosites are not representative of all sites contributing to the signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 provide methodological insights. The advantage of far-Western for multiply phosphorylated proteins (C89) is well-reasoned and supported by citations. The feedback interpretation (C90-C91) is appropriately speculative. The explanation for MS/far-Western discrepancies (C92) is logical and important for interpreting the data.

results.result: Clustering plays a role in the apparent delay in reaching maximal SH2 binding in vivo, and this delay may be a natural feature of SH2-membrane interactions. Clustering of pY binding sites should significantly slow diffusion-limited reaction rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 present the mechanistic interpretation of the findings. The role of clustering (C95) is well-supported by the experimental data (C69-C82). The suggestion that this is a natural feature (C96) is appropriately tentative. The biophysical reasoning about diffusion-limited kinetics (C97) is sound.

results.result: The sustained, clustering-dependent increase in SH2 binding might regulate ERK activation duration. Clustering-dependent recruitment may diversify response kinetics, and phosphorylation of scaffolding proteins like GAB1 and SHCA may increase spatiotemporal diversity of receptor output.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are speculative interpretations about functional consequences. While the timing of ERK activation (C37) is consistent with the hypothesis (C98), no direct evidence links clustering to ERK duration. The ideas about kinetic diversification (C99-C100) are plausible but require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: Full-length GRB2 and the isolated SH2 domain showed similar in vivo membrane binding behavior, indicating that kinetics are dominated by SH2-pY interactions for this protein.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 cites previous work (Oh et al., 2012) to justify using isolated SH2 domains for in vivo studies. This is important for interpreting the live cell imaging data, as it validates that the isolated domain recapitulates full-length protein behavior for at least one key protein.
